title: Reliability Signal Contracts and Deployment Staffing Grid
content:
Purpose and scope:
This note defines a compact, operational set of signal contracts (what we measure, how we measure it, and who owns it) tied directly to deployment staffing obligations and escalation commitments for model serving and inference platforms. The doc is deliberately pragmatic: short, prescriptive agreements to remove ambiguity during incidents and planned rollouts.

Audience:
- Platform engineering leads
- SREs and oncall rotations
- Product & feature owners responsible for model rollout
- Observability and telemetry engineers

Principles (short):
1) Signals must be owned end-to-end: metric, alert, runbook owner. No orphan metrics.
2) Contracts should be small (3–5 SLIs per critical service) and map to clear operational actions.
3) Staffing obligations are matched to risk windows (deploy, peak traffic, post-rollout 72h).
4) Escalation paths are explicit and tested quarterly.

Signal contract template (one-paragraph, canonical):
- Service: model-serving-prod-us-central (example)
- SLI: p95 response time for completion events (end-to-end request -> last token)
- Measurement window and method: 5m rolling, histogram from trace span "generation_complete", exclude warmup probes and synthetic traffic; sampling 100% for first 10s of a rollout, 5% steady state
- Thresholds: warning when p95 > 1800ms for 5m, critical when p95 > 3000ms for 3m
- Owner: eng-serving-runtime/team (primary), observability (secondary)
- Action: on warning, notify feature owner and SRE rotation; on critical, trigger rollback guard in rollout controller and page SRE on-call
- Runbook id: RB-serve-01

Operational staffing grid (textual):
- Pre-deploy (24h before traffic switch): feature owner + release engineer + observability eng on async standby (Slack watch)
- Deploy window (0h to +4h): on-call SRE (primary), platform-release lead (secondary), feature owner in-channel and reachable
- Immediate post-deploy (4h to 72h): reduced cadence on-call (SRE) with nightly checkpoints; feature owner on-call rotation for first 24h if high-risk
- Peak traffic contingency: if traffic delta > 2x baseline, escalate to incident commander and bring in capacity engineering + dedicated GPU ops

Practical examples of signal contracts (three short, unlike canonical above):
1) Throughput signal (SLO candidate)
   - SLI: tokens/sec processed per GPU pool (aggregate)
   - Measurement: 1m rolling average from exporter derived from runtime counters
   - Thresholds: warning if tokens/sec < expected_pool_capacity * 0.8 for 10m; critical if < 0.5 for 5m
   - Owner: dedicated-capacity team
   - Action: trigger autoscale policy & page platform ops

2) Cache hit quality (quality-affecting signal)
   - SLI: prefix cache hit ratio for top-10th percentile requests by rps
   - Measurement: sample traces, compute ratio over 15m, exclude synthetic tests
   - Thresholds: warning < 35%, critical < 20%
   - Owner: serving-runtime + optimize team
   - Action: roll back quantization config change, notify model-owner, run targeted evals

3) Model correctness drift (user-facing quality)
   - SLI: regression rate against golden prompts (anchor set) measured every deploy and hourly during first 24h
   - Measurement: server-side eval harness, threshold is absolute regression > 2%
   - Owner: applied-ml + product-hosted-api
   - Action: immediate rollback and postmortem

Escalation ladder (compact):
- Pager -> SRE rotation (15m) -> Platform lead (30m) -> Feature owner and Product (60m) -> Exec notified after persistent critical for 120m
- During high-impact incidents the incident commander assumes cadence and frees on-call for tactical mitigations

Runbook linking and maintenance:
- Every signal entry must include a runbook id and a short validation script (how to run a quick smoke check).
- Runbooks are reviewed when a signal changes or quarterly otherwise.

Decision rules for adding or removing signals:
- Add when a repeated incident or close-call shows missing observability for a critical action.
- Remove if signal noise > 40% of pages and no actionable remediation is possible.
- Archive signals used only for episodic experiments; require brief owners and re-onboarding path.

Risk matrix (text summary):
- High risk: model correctness regressions, p95 latency spikes, sustained capacity loss. Required staffing: full incident crew + exec comms
- Medium risk: elevated error rates in non-critical routes, partial degradation of embeddings. Required staffing: SRE rotation + feature owner standby
- Low risk: transient retries, degraded metrics with quick self-healing. Required staffing: async triage

Inter-team coordination rituals (weekly / monthly suggestions):
- Weekly 30m "signal sync" between observability, serving-runtime, platform-release to discuss changelists that touch measurement, thresholds, or owners
- Monthly tabletop: 60m rotation-runthrough for one signal (owner runs a mock incident)
- Quarterly review: SLI/alert pruning session (tie to cost and pager metrics)

Unresolved questions / open items (notes to self):
- How to best represent sampled vs full telemetry for SDK-based SDK-instrumented clients (cost vs fidelity). Action: ask Evelyn to prototype 1-week sampling experiment.
- Define explicit policy for synthetic traffic labeling so we never contaminate SLO windows. (Marco to draft)
- Should we collapse some runbooks for similar actions (e.g., latency rollback) or keep fully service-specific? Pros/cons in comments below.

Short rollout checklist for new SLOs / signals (minimal):
1) Create signal doc (this template) + runbook id
2) Add dashboards and test synthetic checks (green/red)
3) Tie to on-call rotation and staffing grid for first 72h
4) Run a canary with 100% sampling for 2h, evaluate metrics and noise
5) Move to steady-state sampling and cadence

Acceptance criteria for this initiative (how we'll know it's working):
- Every high-priority service has an assigned signal contract and runbook (target: 90% coverage within 8 weeks).
- Number of ambiguous incident escalations (where owner not clear) reduced to < 5% of total incidents in a quarter.
- Reduction in false-positive pages from noisy SLI definitions by 30% after signal pruning round

Next steps (who does what):
- Aisha (owner): consolidate feedback and schedule the first signal-sync (target 2026-09-22)
- Marco: draft synthetic labeling policy (due 2026-09-29)
- Evelyn: prototype sampling experiment and cost estimate (due 2026-10-07)
- Jonas: prepare a dashboard template and a runbook checklist (due 2026-09-28)
- Priya: coordinate with product-hosted-api to list top 12 services that must meet coverage target (due 2026-09-24)

Appendix (quick reference snippets):
- Example JQ query for p95 from traces: traces | group_by(service) | map({service: .[0].service, p95: (. | map(.duration) | sort | .[(. | length * 95 / 100) | floor])})
- Simple smoke test for cache hit: curl -H 'x-synthetic:true' https://api.redwood.ai/health/cache-check -> expect JSON {"cache_hit": true}

Notes and tone: this doc is intentionally concise and operational. Expect it to evolve into a set of small signal-contract docs stored in Confluence with runbook ids and links to dashboards. For now, the focus is to force ownership and define minimal staffing commitments so rollouts and incidents have a predictable human response.

Comments: open for edits — explicitly looking for pushback on sampling strategy and the 72h high-risk window duration.
